title: Fired in 1966, Raymond Ackerman Bought Four Small Cape Town Stores
dek: Sacked as head of Checkers after clashing with his board, Raymond Ackerman staked his severance, a loan and friends' money on four small shops called Pick n Pay.

story.event: Being fired as head of Checkers and buying four small Cape Town stores trading as Pick n Pay
story.summary: In 1966 Raymond Ackerman, 35, was fired as head of the 85-store Checkers supermarket chain by the Greatermans group after clashes with its board, which Pick n Pay attributes to his wish to lower prices. With his severance pay, a bank loan, a small inheritance and shares bought by friends, he and his wife Wendy bought four small Cape Town stores trading as Pick n Pay; the company dates its founding to 1967 and listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange in September 1968.
paragraphs: In 1966 Raymond Ackerman, thirty-five, ran Checkers, the supermarket chain of South Africa's Greatermans group. He had once been handed one of its four stores, in Boksburg, and had grown the chain to eighty-five. That year his father, Gus, died, and the Greatermans board fired him. Pick n Pay's own account says it was for wanting to lower prices for customers; a 1999 profile describes constant differences with the board over his adventurous approach to retailing.

His convictions went back to the University of Cape Town in 1948, where, as he recalled, the economist W. H. Hutt "hammered into us consumer sovereignty". His father had warned him that a businessman who only looked after the consumer would be a nice guy but left behind. Later, in the United States, Ackerman studied supermarket methods with Bernardo Trujillo of NCR, who taught him to picture a business as a table with the customer sitting on top.

Now he was out of work with a young family. Recalling it decades later, he kept returning to one fact: "I had four kids." His daughter Suzanne remembered three children and a fourth on the way. He decided to start again on his own. With two weeks' severance pay, a bank loan, a modest inheritance and shares bought by friends, he and his wife, Wendy, bought four small Cape Town grocery stores already trading as Pick n Pay; the company puts the price at R620,000. Suzanne later called it "an enormous gamble" and said he could not have done it without Wendy's support.

Pick n Pay dates its founding to 1967. Almost at once Ackerman began campaigning against price-fixing and monopolies, which earned him the hostility of competitors and the loyalty of shoppers. Checkers, by one account, threw everything it had at the newcomer, pushing him to expand faster than he might have chosen, first to Port Elizabeth and then to Johannesburg. In September 1968 Pick n Pay listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange.

quote.text: Therefore all in the world delight to exalt him and do not weary of him.  Because he does not strive, no one finds it possible to strive with him.
quote.source_title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics, tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #216
quote.connection: Laozi's ruler meets no resistance because he does not strive. Ackerman strove openly, against cartels, price-fixing and the chain that had fired him, and he paid in hostility as well as winning loyalty. The story cannot say whether a quieter way would have cost him less, or achieved less.

reflection: Ackerman lost his job for the thing he did best, and what he remembered afterwards was not wounded pride but a family to provide for. He did not wait to feel certain. He took what he had, a severance cheque, a loan, friends who trusted him and Wendy's backing, and put it into four small shops.

Laozi asks a different question from the one this story usually answers: not how to win a fight, but which fights are needed at all. You may be carrying one at the moment. It is worth asking whether it is central to what you are building, or mainly to how you feel.
invitation: Think of one disagreement at work you have been carrying. Decide today whether it is central to what you are building; if it is not, let it rest for a week.

cross_checks.claim: Ackerman was fired by the Greatermans group in 1966 while running Checkers, then 85 stores
He bought four small Cape Town stores trading as Pick n Pay with his severance pay, a bank loan and friends' backing
Pick n Pay dates its founding to 1967
Pick n Pay listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange in September 1968

research_notes: Year of purchase: the firing is dated 1966 everywhere; the SAHO profile (Bell, 1999) says Pick 'n Pay was founded in 1966, while the company, the SA Jewish Report and IOL date the start to 1967; the story says Ackerman was fired in 1966 and that the company dates its founding to 1967. Children: Ackerman, quoted in the 1999 profile, says 'I had four kids'; his daughter Suzanne told the SA Jewish Report he had three children and one on the way; the story gives both. Reason for dismissal: the company says he was fired for wanting to lower prices; the 1999 profile describes constant differences with the board over his adventurous approach and speculates that Norman Herber felt freer to act after Gus Ackerman's death; the SA Jewish Report says clashes with the board. The story gives the company's version and the profile's, and leaves out the speculation about Herber. The seller, Jack Goldin, is named only in sources that could not be used (Wikipedia, and BusinessTech, which blocks automated requests), so he is not named. The R620,000 price is the company's figure (IOL repeats it); no independent figure was found. Accounts of Ackerman's Checkers start differ (put in charge of launching Checkers in 1955 per the company; chief executive from 1959 per the SA Jewish Report), so the story does not date it. An unverified claim that about fifty friends and relatives backed him is not used. Funding is marked bootstrapped: severance, savings, a bank loan, an inheritance and shares bought by friends, with no institutional investors before the 1968 listing. Ackerman's memoir Hearing Grasshoppers Jump was not available online and is not used. Gus Ackerman's warning is paraphrased from Raymond's recollection in the 1999 profile.
